rss_3_1792447714.title: US government probe into postdoc visas worries scientists
rss_3_1792447714.text:
Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, is under federal investigation for its employment of people holding J-1 visas.Credit: Joe Buglewicz/Bloomberg/Getty

A US investigation into nine universities’ employment of international researchers is prompting concerns among academics at the campuses.

The investigation is focused on the universities’ use of J-1 visas, the main visa used by international postdoctoral researchers. The probe’s purpose is to reduce “visa fraud”, according to vice-president JD Vance.

“They’re using these visas way too much,” Vance said when announcing the investigation on 8 October. “They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”

Critics say that the rationale for the investigation is flawed, that international postdocs play a crucial part in US laboratories and that the announcement is deepening the sense of unease felt by international scientists.

US proposes $100,000 charge for international students to do post-graduate work

“For folks who are not US citizens, it’s pretty dire. It really makes people nervous,” says Theresa Desrochers, a neuroscientist at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, whose lab has hosted a number of visa-holding postdocs over the years. “It just contributes to an overall mood of ‘you’re not wanted here’.”

The US Department of Labor said it does not comment on active investigations.

The institutions under investigation are Harvard, Stanford, Arizona State, Yale and Brown universities; the Massachusetts Institute of Technology; the California Institute of Technology; the University of California, Davis; and the University of Pittsburgh.

When asked for comment, all of the universities except Harvard, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, responded before Nature’s deadline. Many said that they had already received a subpoena asking for information, and many emphasized that they comply with all rules and regulations surrounding visas. “Brown’s international scholars, students and employees make essential contributions on our campus, including to teaching and research that advances American innovation, competitiveness and economic vitality,” says Brian Clark, vice-president of strategic campus communications at Brown.

Numbers game

J-1 visas allow people from outside the United States to study or work in educational or cultural exchanges for a limited time, before returning to their home country. Another visa used by international postdocs and faculty members is the H-1B, which allows them to be hired in specialized fields, including in academia, when job vacancies cannot be filled with the US workforce.

The US Department of Labor’s Office of Inspector General’s press release about the investigation said that about 61% of postdoctoral workers and researchers supported by federal grants at these nine universities are “foreign nationals”, compared with 38% at other institutions. “Something weird is going on at these universities,” said Vance. The department did not respond to questions about the source of those numbers.

Nobel-winning chemist leaves US to direct AI materials lab in China

According to the US National Science Foundation, of the nearly 70,000 science, engineering and health postdocs employed at US universities in 2024, 58% held temporary visas. The National Postdoctoral Association says its own data also show an average of around 60% across all disciplines. Stanford University in California has reported that 66% of its postdocs are international; with the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania reporting 58%; and MIT in Cambridge reporting 65–70%.

Whatever the figures, “a university’s proportion of international researchers relative to a national average does not establish that anyone has been underpaid or that a visa programme has been misused”, says Veena Dubal, general counsel of the American Association of University Professors, a union and membership association of academic professionals in Washington DC.

Even if these nine universities do employ proportionately more international students than other institutions, it’s possible that they attract high numbers of international applicants, says legal scholar Sheldon Evans at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri.

Follow the money

rss_4_1792447715.title: Microdosing LSD shows some cognitive benefits — but only for women
rss_4_1792447715.text:
The human brain’s response to psychedelic drugs is intriguing.Credit: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis via Getty

In a small preliminary study, women who received 15 micrograms of the psychedelic drug LSD focused for longer periods and responded faster to a stimulus than did those who were given a placebo. This effect was not observed for male participants.

The study was presented on 12 October at a neuropsychology meeting, the ECNP Congress in Munich, Germany, by psychopharmacologist Iva Totomanova at Maastricht University in the Netherlands and her colleagues. The findings are “very cool”, says Conor Murray, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “This work is a notable addition to emerging evidence that low doses of LSD have cognitive benefits.” The data also suggest that some people might be more sensitive than others to small quantities of psychedelics, he adds.

Brain boost

'Microdosing' involves taking small doses of a psychedelic every few days, purportedly to improve mood and cognitive function. A typical microdose of LSD can be roughly one-tenth of the amount needed to produce a full psychedelic experience. Although proponents report experiencing a brighter mood and sharper focus, controlled studies on the effects of microdosing have shown mixed results1,2.

Previous research from some members of the team, in collaboration with others, suggests that women feel the drug’s influence more strongly than men3. To find out whether this can be measured objectively, for example in tests of cognitive performance, Totomanova and her colleagues reanalysed data from a previous study that explored the effects of low doses of LSD on 53 healthy people4.

Source: Iva Totomanova et al.

For the new analysis, the researchers focussed on 48 participants. Half of the participants received 15 micrograms of LSD four times over two weeks; others received a placebo. The participants completed a set of cognitive tests assessing sustained attention, information processing and working memory at the beginning of the study, after the first and fourth doses and at a follow-up a week after the last dose. The study was double-anonymized: neither the participants nor the researchers knew who had received the drug.

During the 10-minute test of sustained attention, which involved responding to signals as they appeared on a screen, women who had taken a microdose of LSD reacted 8% faster than those who had been given a placebo. They also experienced fewer attention lapses (see ‘Microdose magic’). By contrast, a microdose of LSD didn’t have much effect on men's reaction time.

rss_5_1792447716.title: How pregnancy reshapes the brain throughout life
rss_5_1792447716.text:
A Mother’s Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution Susana Carmona MIT Press (2026)

When I acquired a copy of the book A Mother’s Brain by neuroscientist Susana Carmona, I thought: at last, a book about what happens to your brain during pregnancy. I recalled how I’d realized in 1997, when I was a young assistant professor, soon after giving birth to my first child, that books for expectant or new parents were light on what happens to the brain. As a neuroscientist, I was curious. What was going on with my brain?

How menopause reshapes the brain

Another observation that I had was how jarring it was to go from having so much attention being paid to me when I was pregnant — including intrusive attention about what I was consuming and unwanted hands on my belly — to the utter lack of attention on me after my baby was born. All of the attention went from pregnant me to the baby. Fair enough, babies can be cute, but what about the mum? What was happening to me? Clearly things in my brain were different, but there was little in the scientific literature to tell me what was happening — which is one of the big reasons I started to work in this area of neuroscience.

My first study on this topic (L. A. Galea et al. Horm. Behav. 37, 86–95; 2000), was about memory and changes in the volume of the hippocampus, a region of the brain, throughout pregnancy. Fast forward two years to me being pregnant with my second child, and I could not for the life of me find where I had parked my car at the end of the day. It was not unusual to find me crying in the stairwell of a ten-storey car park because I was about to be late to pick up kid number one from childcare.

In my experience, mums are often told that our bodies will ‘bounce back’ after pregnancy. But work from Carmona and others now suggests that pregnancy can leave lasting signatures on the brain and body. This will probably not shock any parent, particularly the one who gave birth.

A remarkable transition

A Mother’s Brain is, in many ways, an ode to the remarkable ‘plasticity’ or adaptability of the brain and body during and after pregnancy. Gestation requires adaptations across almost every physiological system, and Carmona describes these changes to the cardiovascular, immune and circulatory systems exceptionally well. The book also details the remarkable role of the placenta in orchestrating many of these adaptations. When considering this physiological transformation, it’s no surprise that pregnancy also leaves a signature on the brain.

Embryos share cells with the parent through the placenta.Credit: OMIKRON/SPL

Carmona conveys her palpable love of being a mother while recognizing that motherhood is not universally joyful. I agree strongly with Carmona’s contention that people need to be truthful with parents-to-be. The experience isn’t always positive. Some people will experience mental-health challenges during this period, possibly for the first time.

It is important that they seek — and receive — the support that they need. Care during pregnancy and in the postpartum period must attend to mental as well as physical health, and timely access to effective treatments, including talk therapy, should be standard. The repercussions of not receiving enough support can be tragic.

The book is at its best when Carmona conveys just how biologically extraordinary pregnancy is. For example, she describes how cells from a baby can linger in the bodies of people who have been pregnant, sometimes for decades, yet it is still not known how these cells contribute to long-term health. Carmona also takes the reader through the genesis of her own research questions and the paths they took from idea to publication, interspersing the science with anecdotes from her life and pregnancies.

What drugs are safe during pregnancy? There’s a shocking lack of data

Yet, I found myself wishing that Carmona had gone into more detail about another part of this story: how difficult it has been to convince the scientific community that pregnancy’s effects on the brain are worth studying. Carmona’s first landmark paper on this topic (E. Hoekzema et al. Nature Neurosci. 20, 287–296; 2017) did not have an easy path to publication. I know this first-hand. I was one of the reviewers who argued with the editors about the importance and novelty of the work.

There are many hidden obstacles to publishing research on women’s health, even though the paucity of existing research might suggest the opposite, given that new findings are paramount for getting your work accepted. Many researchers in the field need to justify that their findings are worth publishing. I would have welcomed more exploration of that resistance and why questions concerning pregnancy and the brain are often overlooked.

Discussion of what these pregnancy-related brain changes mean is also important. These are natural adaptations. For example, people often experience a reduction in brain volume during gestation. But this is not necessarily a bad thing, just as an increase is not necessarily good. Different brain regions and measures (such as volume and connectivity) change in various ways during pregnancy and in the postpartum period, and the overall effects can be confusing to piece together. But such distinctions are, as Carmona points out, important for a public audience for whom headlines about a ‘shrinking brain’ can sound alarming.

Parallels with other species

Consider the hippocampus. A Mother’s Brain describes this region but pays relatively little attention to the striking parallels between human findings and decades of work in other mammals. These studies have shown that rodents experience pregnancy-related and postpartum changes to cognition, to the structure of the hippocampus and to the creation of nerve cells in the brain. In rats, the production of neurons decreases during pregnancy and the early postpartum period, with subtle variations between first and second pregnancies. There are also later differences between foster mothers and birthing mothers in terms of brain-cell creation in the hippocampus and memory that remain to be explained.

In the long term, beyond the postpartum period, reproductive experience improves memory and the plasticity of the hippocampus because it results in changes to nerve-cell quantity and connections throughout life. That paradox — decreases in one measure alongside improved function in others — is why interpreting pregnancy-related brain changes requires more than asking whether a measure went up or down.

rss_6_1792447718.title: Climate scientists face deluge of public-records requests about fossil-fuel studies
rss_6_1792447718.text:
Protestors demonstrate outside the US Supreme Court on 5 October, as justices hear a case whose outcome could determine whether fossil-fuel companies can be held responsible for global warming.Credit: Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty

Last month, a climate scientist working in the University of California system received an unsettling message from her institution. University officials asked her to submit all correspondence related to a study she had published linking emissions from fossil fuels to environmental harms caused by climate change. The university had received a public-records request from a law firm representing the Patriots Foundation in Des Moines, Iowa, which describes itself on its website as a government watchdog.

It was the fifth such request connected to the organization that the scientist, who requested anonymity to avoid further demands, had received this year.

Heatwaves linked to carbon emissions from specific companies

The requests seem to be part of an expanding effort by groups with ties to the energy industry to discredit findings in the burgeoning field of climate attribution science, which estimates the extent to which extreme weather events, such as floods and heatwaves, are due to climate change. The demands come at a time when attribution science’s role in lawsuits against major industrial emitters is growing.

An investigation by Nature has identified at least 30 requests for correspondence relating to climate attribution science that researchers in the United States say they have received since 2024. These requests, involving the Patriots Foundation and other groups, have gone to 13 public universities and involved the correspondence of dozens of climate scientists, legal scholars and attorneys. Last month, the news outlet Politico reported that it had identified more than 100 open-records requests made to researchers since 2021, related more broadly to lawsuits about damages caused by climate change, rather than just to climate attribution research. It’s unclear how many of these requests overlap.

Neither the Patriots Foundation nor the law firm representing it responded to Nature’s queries about the reason for the requests, or about researchers’ concerns over them. Another organization that has submitted requests — called Government Accountability and Oversight, based in Sheridan, Wyoming — directed Nature to blog posts saying that attribution researchers are activists opposing the fossil-fuel industry and that, if they have the right to do “this sort of lobbying”, “the rest of us have a right to see the receipts under state transparency laws”.

Climate science is supporting lawsuits that could help save the world

Recipients say that the timing of the requests and the information they ask for suggest that their purpose is to fish for conflicts of interest that could be used to discredit the scientists’ findings. A hypothetical example of such a conflict might be attorneys paying a climate scientist to conduct a particular study. The researchers think the requests might also be attempts to collect information about collaborators and contacts who are not subject to public-records laws, such as scientists and attorneys at private institutions.

Requests of this kind are legal. And Nature spoke to several recipients who say they have nothing to hide. They emphasize that communicating with attorneys involved in climate litigation does not bias their work or represent a conflict of interest.

But some say that the volume of requests seems intended to dissuade work on climate attribution, and wastes time and public money. They also say that if scientists know that any e-mail discussion with a colleague might become the subject of an investigation or taken out of context, that could suppress open scientific debate. “It’s annoying. It’s harassment,” says the University of California climate scientist.

Climate in the court

Studies linking climate change in general to certain weather events have been conducted since 20041. But only in the past several years have researchers begun to use their climate models to estimate how much the emissions from particular companies contributed to specific ‘damages’, such as deaths caused by a heat wave.

Dozens of climate-related lawsuits that are now working their way through the US courts could hinge on whether judges or juries agree that such ‘source attribution’ research is rigorous. That includes a case involving the US energy company Suncor and representatives of Boulder County in Colorado, heard by the US Supreme Court this month. The outcome could determine whether similar lawsuits proceed in state courts.

Climate attribution science estimates the extent to which extreme weather events, such as the wildfire in Boulder, Colorado, shown here, are due to climate change.Credit: Michael Ciaglo/Getty

Researchers say that the legal relevance of attribution science has made the field a political target. For instance, a Republican-led committee of the US Congress has investigated a chapter in a reference manual for federal judges that explains attribution science, alleging it represents an improper attempt by climate activists to influence judges. US President Donald Trump, a Republican who is friendly towards the fossil-fuel industry and has called climate change a hoax, weighed in, declaring the chapter “fraudulent, biased, and misleading” on social media.

“Climate attribution is under attack,” says Christopher Callahan, a climate scientist at Indiana University Bloomington. In May, he received a public-records request from Government Accountability and Oversight to review his correspondence with eight individuals involved in climate litigation.

‘It’s totally a surge’

The volume of requests for climate researchers has noticeably increased this year, says Lauren Kurtz at the Climate Science Legal Defense Fund in New York City, an organization that helps scientists to address legal issues in this field. “It’s totally a surge,” she adds.

rss_7_1792447719.title: ‘Fiercely stubborn’: the US scientists continuing their research amid funding cuts
rss_7_1792447719.text:
Equity. Racial discrimination. Climate change. Gender. These are just a few of the 200 or so terms being used to flag federal grants that are under review to determine whether they align with the research priorities set by the administration of US President Donald Trump. The administration initially terminated US$3 billion in grants in 2025, and despite many reversals, roughly $1.4 billion in funding from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF) remained frozen or cancelled earlier this year. In addition, roughly $25 billion for international aid and development — including for research on global health, infectious-disease surveillance and environmental conservation — was lost when the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was closed down last year.

During the first two years of Trump’s second term, amid funding cuts, agency and programme closures and lawsuits (see ‘Lost funding and shut-down science’), some researchers had to get creative to keep their research moving in a productive direction. Many have turned to private donations or crowdfunding; others tweaked their focus or explored interdisciplinary collaborations. Some have even been wildly successful at spinning their research animals into viral Internet eye candy to raise awareness and funds (see Nature https://doi.org/rsk4; 2026).

Lost funding and shut-down science Selected major developments and policies from US President Donald Trump’s administration that have led to a loss of resources and funding. 20 January 2025: Executive Order 14169 initiates stop-work orders amid a government-wide 90-day review of all foreign development assistance, effectively halting grants for global-health projects funded by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s International Affairs grants for conservation research. 21 January 2025: Executive Order 14173 directs the dismantling of diversity, equity and inclusion policies, programmes, preferences and activities across the federal government. January to March 2025: USAID funds are frozen; its website and most programmes are shut down, with the termination of 5,200 contracts and grants. 14 February 2025: The US Office of Personnel Management begins a mass reduction in the federal workforce; nearly 25,000 probationary federal workers were affected in the early stages. 28 February 2025: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) starts to terminate research grants. 18 April 2025: The National Science Foundation starts to terminate research grants. April and May 2025: Individual researchers, the American Public Health Association, Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality and other organizations file lawsuits against the NIH over grant terminations. June 2025: The Climate.gov website disappears. 1 August 2025: A US district court rules in the GLMA: Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality v. NIH case that the NIH cannot terminate grants related to research on the health of people from sexual and gender minorities and orders funding to be reinstated.

Nature’s careers team spoke to six researchers about how they kept their work going strong and their teams resilient despite the government scrutiny. Although some funders — the NIH, USAID, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the US Department of the Interior (DOI) — did not respond to Nature’s requests for responses to these accounts of lost funding, the NSF stated that the Trump administration’s current budget priorities and goals “reduce administrative burden on researchers, broaden access to funding opportunities, and better match the structure of awards to the character of the research being supported”. In addition, a White House spokesperson said in a statement to Nature: “The Trump administration remains committed to ensuring that taxpayer dollars fund research that actually can benefit everyday Americans and is not ideologically grounded.”

JOSH PLOTNIK: Cultivate interdisciplinary collaborations

Elephant-cognition researcher at Hunter College, the City University of New York, New York.

My laboratory group studies Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) in Thailand. We research both the evolution of intelligence, to understand how different animals adapt to a rapidly changing world, and interventions to reduce human–elephant conflict. Two of my group’s grants were frozen when the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s International Affairs grants were suspended in February 2025. The cumulative impact on global wildlife conservation efforts was substantial.

Meeting the moment: how scientific philanthropies are expanding their reach

We, like many researchers, turned to philanthropy and fundraisers. Hunter College in New York City held a fundraiser to support several research and education programmes. I also received a grant from the Templeton World Charity Foundation in Nassau, the Bahamas, and support for my staff in Thailand comes, in part, from the Golden Triangle Asian Elephant Foundation in Chiang Rai. But many researchers are chasing the same pots of philanthropic funding.

To secure US federal support, I’m currently exploring interdisciplinary research projects to study how cognition changes across an elephant’s lifetime and how those changes might compare with what occurs in humans. Elephants might offer a particularly valuable comparative model because of their long lifespans, complex social lives and sophisticated problem-solving abilities. I think ambitious multidisciplinary teams are key to the type of groundbreaking research that will secure NSF or NIH funding. Collaboration has always been important, but it’s even more so now. Why compete, if instead, you can collaborate and push the boundaries of science?

Eranga Galappaththi (left) has pivoted to US-based research on climate and food.Credit: Sithuni M. Jayasekara

ERANGA GALAPPATHTHI: Establish a track record of US-focused research

Climate-adaptation researcher at Virginia Tech in Blacksburg.

My research team has spent the past decade building relationships with Indigenous peoples’ networks to co-produce research about how climate change is affecting, for example, hunting and gathering activities in the Canadian Arctic and Sri Lanka. Our original goal was to do a large-scale comparative analysis of fisheries systems and how they’ve been affected by climate change in the two regions. In April 2025, we lost more than $400,000 in NSF funds.

US science after a year of Trump: what has been lost and what remains

We had another pending grant from the Belmont Forum, an international partnership of funders focused on environmental sustainability. That funding helped us to maintain research relationships with our Indigenous community partners. In community-engaged Indigenous research, trust is built by showing up consistently, following through on commitments, returning results to communities and developing the research together rather than simply arriving to collect data and then leaving. When funding suddenly disappears, activities that communities were expecting might be delayed, reduced or cancelled — and community members might not realize the distinction between a research team changing its plans and a funding agency terminating support. So far, our partners have remained supportive and interested in continuing the collaborations. But maintaining those relationships becomes much more difficult without stable funding.

Now that the NSF has shifted its priorities away from knowledge-co-production with Indigenous communities, I’m reworking research proposals. The current NSF strategic plan emphasizes topics such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, biotechnology innovation and quantum-information science. And because funding for international research has dwindled, I need to establish a track record of US-focused research.

To that end, I’m doing some original analyses on food-system vulnerabilities and health outcomes using existing publicly available data sets. These data are related to climate, food systems, health, demographics and socio-economic conditions. We are also developing systematic-review and meta-analysis projects to identify broader patterns, effect sizes and sources of variation that might not be visible from individual studies. These approaches help my team to ask original research questions and produce scientific knowledge with fewer resources than would be required for field-based data collection. These approaches are adaptations to the current funding environment, not substitutes for community-engaged research. But I’ll also be doing the slow work of building collaborations with Alaska-based communities.

Rebecca Lindsey started an effort to keep US climate data online and accessible.

REBECCA LINDSEY: Crowdsource to preserve reliable data

Project director for Climate.us, a public climate-information website affiliated with the non-profit organization Multiplier, based in San Francisco, California.

More than one million people were visiting the Climate.gov website every month until, after nearly 15 years, it disappeared in June 2025. At the time, the account had more than 500,000 followers on social-media platforms. It was run by NOAA and I thought of it as a climate-literacy warehouse in which users could view a dashboard of global climate-change and climate-variability data, see maps showing projected changes in US temperatures in coming decades and get scientist-vetted answers to questions about the causes and impacts of human-caused global warming.

Inside the new political screening that’s stalling NIH grants

In January 2025, I and other NOAA employees were told by the Trump administration to review Climate.gov and remove content deemed to be in violation of administration policies. For example, the climate-literacy guide used by educators had to be removed because it covered equity. In late February 2025, I was fired by the Department of Government Efficiency, four months before the website was removed. Users are now redirected to a NOAA climate landing page, which doesn’t include the comprehensive dashboards and offers a limited view of what science can tell us about the state of the climate.

In August 2025, I and two other former Climate.gov employees turned to crowdfunding to recreate the effort as the website Climate.us. The non-profit organization Multiplier hosted us, because starting our own non-profit organization would have taken valuable time. Relying mostly on word of mouth, we raised more than $630,000 from various funding platforms.

We also knew that launching a website would create demand for fresh content. We are updating articles, maps and graphics and adding new ones. On top of that, we are restoring the climate-literacy guide, which offered an educational tool to explain core concepts such as greenhouse gases, fossil fuels and ecosystem threats. But I no longer have the expertise of NOAA’s pool of scientists, who used to provide this as part of their jobs. We have about 80 volunteers — academics, non-profit researchers and retired federal scientists — but we certainly don’t have enough depth of expertise in subfields of climate research. We might have to consider paying researchers for that expertise. Going forwards, it would be ideal to host the site on a platform that could partner flexibly with the government at all levels — federal, state and tribal — and that would remain protected from political decisions.

Sharon Hillier turned to funds from private donors to salvage HIV clinical-trial samples from Africa.

SHARON HILLIER: Find donors to help salvage samples

Expert in reproductive infectious diseases at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania.

My work focuses on how best to prevent sexually transmitted diseases. Over the past three years, my colleagues and I have been working on drug-based products to prevent HIV infection, focusing on three African countries. The nine-year project had a total cost of $205 million, and was funded by USAID in 2024. But on 27 February 2025, we received a termination letter that stated that our research award “is not aligned with Agency priorities”. As a result, we lost $138 million. At the time, I had hundreds of samples from three clinical-trial sites in Zimbabwe, Kenya and South Africa where we were testing combinations of antivirals and contraceptives. We had no way to cover our collaborators’ costs for either long-term storage of the samples or shipping them to the United States for analysis. I asked USAID for $20,000 to ship the samples to my lab. During a call, USAID staff asked me whether it would be cheaper to burn or to ship the samples; I responded “to burn them”.

‘Shattered’: US scientists speak out about how Trump policies disrupted their careers

Without those samples, we were on the verge of losing the results from the three clinical trials. I thought about calling it quits and retiring, but scientists are fiercely stubborn and driven to do good research. So, I started looking for ways to keep this research alive.

rss_8_1792447720.title: Experienced researchers ‘disrupt’ less than rookie scientists — but their ideas last
rss_8_1792447720.text:
Physicist Mildred Dresselhaus with a student; a study has found that more experienced scientists produce more persistently disruptive science than their younger peers.Credit: Micheline Pelletier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Experienced scientists produce ‘disruptive’ work less often than early-career researchers, but when they do, their innovations are more likely to have a lasting effect, according to a study1 published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on 19 October.

Previous research has suggested that experienced scientists are less likely to produce disruptive work2 — discoveries that overturn established foundations, rather than building on them incrementally — than are those starting their careers. The latest findings challenge the view that scientists become less innovative as they age, says Sam Arts, who studies scientific and technological innovation at KU Leuven in Antwerp, Belgium.

The latest study analysed more than 11 million papers published between 1800 and 2022 by around 206,000 scientists globally, all of whom had more than 40 years of research experience. The authors used those papers’ citation patterns as a proxy to measure the extent to which their innovations disrupted previous work, and how likely it was that their findings were displaced by subsequent research.

Citation patterns are often used to measure changes in innovation, but some scientists have questioned whether such metrics can accurately capture the disruptiveness of scientific findings3.

Disruption metrics

The latest study estimated how disruptive a scientific paper is using a measure called the CD index4. This metric is calculated by analysing subsequent citations: is the focal paper cited with its accompanying references, or without them? Or do subsequent studies cite just the focal paper’s references, and not the paper itself? If a paper is cited without its references also being cited, this is a good indication that those references “are no longer relevant”, says co-author An Zeng, who studies the science of science at Beijing Normal University in China.

But the conventional CD index measures only how strongly a paper overturns previous work, and does not consider whether that disruption endures, say the authors. To address this issue, they also used their own metric, called persistent disruption (PD), which identifies highly disruptive papers (using the CD index) and then looks at how much these papers are themselves disrupted by future papers5. A persistently disruptive paper, say the researchers, is one that disrupts previous work and that is not displaced by subsequent research.

Their method involved first identifying a focal paper, and then examining whether subsequent papers cite it directly and/or indirectly (by referencing one of those citing papers). If a later study cites both the original, focal paper and a study that cites it, it shows that the focal paper’s disruptiveness is still there, says co-author Nan Deng, who studies the science of science at the National Science Library of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing.

The study found that the probability of a researcher publishing a highly disruptive paper decreased as their career progressed, but the chance of them publishing a persistently disruptive paper increased over time, from about 1% at the start of their career to about 2.2% after 40 years.

The authors report that scientists who produced persistently disruptive work tended to have published a relatively large number of papers before their disruptive one.

But the findings should not be interpreted as showing that senior scientists are generally more innovative, or that ageing itself causes more durable breakthroughs, says Kenneth Huang, who studies innovation and technology management at the National University of Singapore. Instead, the study suggests that as the number of years that a scientist has been in that career increases, they are more likely to be associated with papers that have a lasting influence, Huang says.

Real-world influence

rss_9_1792447721.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
rss_9_1792447721.text:
Artificial-intelligence systems such as large language models (LLMs) can exhibit behaviour that seems strikingly intelligent. This has led many people, including some experts, to wonder whether these systems could have some form of consciousness — the capacity for subjective experience. However, we think that existing AI systems are not conscious, and that, along current trajectories of development, they are not likely to become conscious. Greater clarity about whether AI could become consciousness will be crucial as society grapples with the challenges posed by this increasingly powerful technology.

Can AI ever be conscious? The question stems from a misconception

Several prominent scientists, including biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, have argued that AI systems might already be conscious. And earlier this year, AI company Anthropic in San Francisco, California, published research claiming to have identified computational signatures of a form of consciousness in its Claude model1.

Whether AI models can ever be conscious is not merely a philosophical question. It has practical implications. For instance, if AI systems were conscious, they might experience distress and pain, similar to how people do. Then should countless new conscious entities that might experience suffering be allowed to proliferate? Perhaps not surprisingly, some people are already calling for ‘AI welfare’ and ‘AI rights’ to be taken seriously2.

Conversely, if AI systems only seem to be conscious and lack actual inner experience, then granting them rights or protections could hinder efforts to govern and control them at precisely the time when oversight is urgently needed. Following this path would draw attention and resources away from beings whose consciousness is not in any doubt.

Looking beyond humans and our closest relatives in the animal kingdom, it is still hard to be certain about what does, and does not, have the capacity for consciousness — be it insects, AI or the creations of synthetic biology, such as laboratory-grown brain organoids3,4.

Why we need mandatory safeguards for emotionally responsive AI

This uncertainty has prompted some researchers to advocate a precautionary approach: if there is a reasonable chance that AI systems could be conscious, then society must take anticipatory action and give those systems some form of protection against potential suffering. This, the argument goes, would avoid reprising moral errors of the past — for example, the mistreatment of non-human animals, or surgery on preterm human babies without anaesthesia. An extreme version of this idea is that society should reallocate resources from addressing the welfare concerns of present-day humans to lessen the potential suffering of trillions of future AI descendants.

In our view, uncertainty is not the same as knowing nothing, and it does not mean that all possibilities are equally likely to occur. Decisions about what is moral must weigh both the consequences of false negatives — failing to recognize consciousness where it exists — and the costs of false positives — attributing consciousness where none exists. In the case of AI, we think that false positives are much more likely to occur than false negatives are. If so, a precautionary approach would be misguided.

Between us, we’ve spent decades studying consciousness from diverse scientific perspectives: experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology and philosophy of mind. On the basis of this work, we feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today’s technologies. Here, we set out three reasons for our scepticism.

Intelligence is not consciousness

What we mean by consciousness is simple enough: it is what goes away with dreamless sleep or under general anaesthesia, and what returns after waking up or while dreaming. Conscious experiences feel like something, whether it is tasting ice cream on a hot day or seeing the vibrant colours of a sunset. Philosopher Thomas Nagel, whose influential 1974 essay ‘What is it like to be a bat?’ helped to shape modern debates about consciousness, arguing that a conscious organism is one for which there is “something that it is like to be that organism”5.

This definition of consciousness introduces the first reason for scepticism about conscious AI. Consciousness is not the same thing as intelligence. Consciousness is about being and feeling; intelligence — very broadly — is all about doing, or performing functions. Just because something is intelligent does not mean that it is conscious.

Humans know that we are conscious, and we tend to associate consciousness with using our intellectual capacities. Yet, conscious experience and intelligent behaviour can come apart in striking ways. We know firsthand that our brain and body can carry out highly intelligent processes wholly outside awareness. For example, the cerebellum adjusts and plans motor performance in a way that is precise, fast and adaptable through ongoing learning. Yet none of what it does involves consciousness directly — we are wholly unaware of all its ‘computations’. Moreover, absence or removal of the cerebellum, which contains nearly four-fifths of the neurons in the human brain, does not affect consciousness directly6.

AI is programmed to hijack human empathy — we must resist that

The temptation to conflate intelligence and consciousness probably reflects baked-in psychological biases — anthropocentrism, viewing the world through a human lens, and anthropomorphism, attributing human characteristics to things that merely resemble people. Consider, for example, the seductive power of language, a capacity that humans have long felt makes us special. When LLMs talk to us, it’s natural to project onto them properties that accompany our linguistic fluency, such as intelligence and consciousness.

But LLMs are trained on vast quantities of human-written text, much of it explicitly or implicitly concerned with thoughts, feelings and conscious experiences. LLMs are mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past7. We gaze into them and all too readily confuse the reflections with our own conscious minds8.

The beguiling nature of LLMs is highlighted by considering the response to AlphaFold9, made by Google DeepMind in London. Similar to an LLM, AlphaFold is a powerful neural network running on silicon hardware. Yet almost nobody worries that it might be conscious. That’s because AlphaFold predicts protein structures, whereas LLMs ‘talk’ to us. The compelling illusion of consciousness created by linguistic fluency just isn’t there for AlphaFold.

Silicon brains

Second, the idea of conscious AI is motivated by the assumption that algorithms running on silicon are, in principle, sufficient for consciousness10. In other words, that computation of the right kind is all that it takes, and that it doesn’t matter whether these computations are implemented inside carbon-based brains or in silicon-based computers. Philosophers call this assumption computational functionalism. Although computations are clearly sufficient to produce forms of intelligence — as modern AI systems demonstrate — it is much less clear that they could also be sufficient for consciousness.

Computational functionalism is widely assumed among members of the tech community and is popular among some scientists and philosophers, too, but we think it is fatally flawed because brains are not — or at least not just — computers that are made of meat.

rss_11_1792447724.title: How to compare and strengthen research systems
rss_11_1792447724.text:
How does a country get the biggest bang for its buck when it comes to science? Comparing science systems between countries can be a good way to see what’s working well and what’s not. But it’s difficult to do.

Want to speed up scientific progress? First understand how science policy works

Different countries analyse different things; relevant data can be hard to find or access; and the same concepts can be defined and measured in various ways.

Scientific outputs such as numbers of publications, citations and patents are easy to quantify. But they say little about what factors influenced them. Standardized statistics published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), for example on investments, allow for easy comparisons between countries. But these measurements are not enough to analyse the intertwined effects that different approaches to funding, running institutions and supporting researchers can have over time. Some metrics — such as how funding shapes researchers’ careers — are rarely measured systematically.

And even when countries report on similar measures, differences in data collection can make comparisons difficult. For example, one country reporting information about its fundamental research might publish detailed spending statistics by sector and funding source; another might report only aggregated spending that includes applied research. This makes it hard to form a coherent global picture.

To overcome these problems, a group that I lead has developed an approach to analysing national research systems — gathering data from a broad range of sources and developing measures for often-overlooked aspects of such systems. I hope that other researchers, funders and international organizations will use our framework, and find ways to improve it.

China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?

Our project, the China Fundamental Research Report, examines research systems in 25 countries and regions, including the European Union (www.cfrr.net). The chosen regions have systems of various sizes, structures and stages of development. In particular, China offers a useful case study because its scientific landscape has transformed over the past 40 years, through sustained investment in funding, institutions, talent and research infrastructure.

Our work was possible thanks to a rapid expansion in the amount of research information that is now openly available — from publication and funding databases to data repositories and more. This has made it much easier to compare many facets of research between countries. We used large-scale computational methods to analyse data sets that were previously difficult to study together.

One key part of our work was developing fresh indicators to capture areas of research that are not usually measured. For example, we used large language models to identify signals of novelty in research questions and methods — how far a study ventures beyond established knowledge. We also linked publications to patent citations to trace connections between fundamental research and technological development. And we combined funding and workforce data to trace how, in China, junior researchers make a substantial contribution to scientific output. This group, we found, was supported by a long-term expansion of funding for early-career researchers from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

rss_12_1792447725.title: Why failure is a taboo topic in science
rss_12_1792447725.text:
Stephen Webster 00:04

But I just want to welcome you, those of you who are external to Imperial.

Of course, those of you who are at Imperial, welcome too.

It’s not often we can get together as colleagues to discuss these kinds of things.

That’s me kicking off the opening session of the Failure in Science conference.

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture and what we don’t.

And of course, being a university, that means conferences.

And this one, Failure in Science, has really got a lot to do with Magdalena Skipper sitting here because she said to me this time last year, ”Should we have a conference on failure in science?”

And I just thought, Imperial College, Nature magazine, a conference about failure. You know, this is really too good to be true. Let’s work on this.

So, and so Magdalena Skipper, (she’s editor-in-chief of the journal Nature), and I got to work.

And in April 2026 at Imperial, we welcomed 150 delegates, all of them eager to talk about something not much talked about: failure in science.

We spent the day focused on stuff going wrong, mistakes being made, opportunities being missed, and good things just being neglected.

In this series of six podcasts, using the conference as a springboard, we’re exploring different aspects of failure.

That means much more than simply looking at failure as something personal, a spot of bad luck coming our way.

When it comes to science, is there institutional failure too? For example, should universities frame failure not as a problem, but as part of a creative process, as part of good science? How can institutions look more sympathetically at failure and see failure as a necessity when quick progress is so often the bottom line.

And we’ll also look at the impact of science more widely. What can go wrong when scientific knowledge leaves the lab and tries to make a difference in society?

But first, in episode one, over to Magdalena Skipper.

Magdalena Skipper 02:41

First of all, actually, I want to start by thanking you and Imperial for following up on what I honestly did not think you were going to follow up on.

Because failure is a taboo topic.

Even though we know that failure is part of success, failure is one of the best teachers that we have, as long as we learn from those failures and don’t repeat those mistakes.

I’m Magdalena Skipper. I am editor-in-chief of Nature.

At the conference, I talked about the fact that failure is often a taboo. We don’t talk about it. We know that in science, failure is an everyday occurrence, and of course, failure itself is a very large umbrella term.

Most experiments fail. We learn from that failure, a great deal. Sometimes our plans in our career fail. We learn from that as well. We have to back up and pivot in another direction.

Considering how useful those lessons are, how contextualized they are, I find it surprising that we don’t talk more about failure, that we’re not more honest about the role that failure plays.

But we are petrified of it.

If you failed, you’re a loser, and that’s why nobody wants to talk about it.

Hence, it’s a taboo.

Failure is part and parcel of our lives, be it professional or personal. We learn through failure. There isn’t a single individual who hasn’t failed at something.

The really crucial aspect of it is how much we learn from it. We learn it’s a matter of building resilience, but it’s a matter also of delving deep into the topic, into the situation in which we have failed, and understanding it much, much more deeply in a much more nuanced way.

So, on the one hand, it’s a natural process. There isn’t a person or a system that hasn’t failed at some point. And on the other hand, it’s such a useful teacher.

The conference was part of a wider project called the Good Science Project, and in the end, the day focused on a number of levels.

One was an individual level. How individuals fail themselves and how they feel about it, how they recover from it, what they learn from it.

We talked about what failing means at an institutional level, or an organizational level.

And of course, since science or research more broadly doesn’t just happen in an academic setting, we also talk about how failure is dealt with in other settings, in the private sector, in in society more broadly.

Much later on in my professional career, I made a decision to step away from scientific, active scientific research and become a scientific editor.

I did that after a PhD and after a postdoc. And now, for me, looking back over the years, I think that was, without a doubt, the best professional decision I ever made. But to some who are wedded to the idea that the only true path for a researcher is to continue in active research, that was a sign of my failure.

I failed to be a successful academic researcher.

And it’s really interesting because that one act, that one action that I took, for me, was a manifestation of success or successful decision, and a manifestation of failure for others.

So I have been referred to as a failed scientist. And of course I’m a failed many other things.

Once upon a time, I wanted to be a firefighter. I’m also a failed firefighter. That never came to pass.

I think the most important thing is that I don’t fail all the time at what I’m actually doing right now.

And perhaps the next thing to add is, in general, in failure, if you do fail, learning from that experience so you move on, and you move on as a richer individual, a richer professional, is really important.

Think about the following example...

If you are constantly petrified of failing, you are going to play safe all the time. You’re not going to take risks. You’re not going to place big bets, if you like.

Now, in science, that translates into addressing big questions, formulating risky hypotheses, deciding to dedicate funding to a risky, perhaps long-term project that is not fail-safe, is not something that, broadly speaking, we already understand, and you colouring in the boxes or filling in the blanks.

No, if you are not afraid of failure, you are more likely to take bigger risks. And of course, when you take bigger risks, yes, there is a risk of failure.

But there is a risk of there’s a possibility of of great of great gain. Now, our general aversion towards failure means that in our funding systems, we tend to we tend to prefer to fund projects that have quite a lot of foundation, that is safe already.

Many scientists have the experience when they apply for grants, that a large proportion of what it is they’re proposing in the grant they already know is going to work because they have demonstrated it at some smaller level to a smaller degree.

So the question then becomes: is our funding system really designed to push the boundaries of knowledge and make us take those risks and discover something completely unknown, take us in a new direction, maybe open a new avenue, maybe even create a new discipline, or uncover a new approach to probing some questions?

Or is it more designed to walk, take very small steps in some direction?

It’s fascinating to consider the different attitudes that different sectors, different industries have towards failure.

But my understanding is it’s a practice that is relatively widespread in technology companies, especially in Silicon Valley.

And the practice is as follows. In order not to stifle and prevent that risk-taking attitude, which may lead to failure, those companies actually reward their employees financially for failing.

But if they fail fast, imagine without this incentive, you have a situation where only the employees-and this is in the research setting within Google X, only the employees that come up with quote unquote ”positive results”, something that can be taken forward, are rewarded.

But those positive results may be less impactful, or less influential, or have fewer implications if all the employees are thinking: Oh, I will only get rewarded if I succeed. I therefore must not fail at all cost.

That really influences your risk taking.

Now, of course, from a company’s perspective, there’s no point investing employees’ time or money in long-term pursuit of a project that fails. So what is being rewarded is fast failure. That is crucial.

That is failing fast. To me, it’s a really interesting way of incentivizing risk-taking.

Basically, ultimately, of course, everyone wants to succeed, but the road to that success often leads through failure, and maybe there isn’t another way. Maybe you have to go through failure in order to get to that success.

And contrasting that to an academic setting, where often a lot of time and money is invested in long-term projects, then there should have been a stop, no go decision made earlier on, but perhaps I’m sure there are a number of reasons why a similar approach is not adopted in academic setting.

But one of them I would suggest is that fear of failure? Once you have a project, it’s your project, it’s your baby. You’ve created it. You need to continue proceeding with it.

At the conference I mentioned one specific example of how failure can really energize and motivate researchers.

So the specific example, it’s an example of a paper, a scientific paper, describes a metascience study, so a science of science, where the researchers obtain data from a funder, a US funder, looking at a population of scientists around the cutoff bar for funding.

So they looked at a small, small sliver of this population just above that cutoff. So individuals who just scraped in and got the funding. And then those individuals who just didn’t make it, who just didn’t get the funding. They followed those researchers through time.

And the really interesting finding is that those who just failed to get the funding did better in terms of their career, establishing their career, and contribution to science, than those who just got the funding.

Now that was an observation in the paper. We can speculate why there might be, but I myself find it particularly compelling to think that it’s almost a demonstration of a saying: What doesn’t kill you make you makes you stronger.

That if you’re really convinced that you have a great idea, that you are committed to pursuing a scientific career, and you failed in gaining this support, financial support, then you will find another way.

And that induces that inventiveness and creates a greater motivation for you to persevere, because you are sure that you need to succeed.

So here, failure gives you a boost, if you like, is an additional motivator.

We all know, we have discussed already, that science progresses through self-correction, through a series of failures. These are learning opportunities.

Every graduate student, every scientist, working scientist in the lab, whether it’s the wet lab, or computational lab, or in the field, knows that a large proportion of experiments are going to fail, and that setup and expectations need to be adjusted.

Maybe the question needs to be modified. Maybe parameters need to be changed. Again, that learning process, that comes out of failure.

But we never talk about it. We never talk about that process, that iteration, that trial and error, (it’s not random. It’s intentional), but it’s there. We never talk about it when we talk about science to the general public.

Sometimes the rhetoric is more reminiscent of religious belief than actually a scientific fact that has been arrived at through that iterative process, stops and starts, and failures, and consolidation of ideas, and changing the hypothesis, etc. etc.

It’s not that the scientists don’t know what they’re doing, that they’re not following the scientific method, they are, but they’re not communicating that to the public.

I think the best example of that was during the pandemic, the COVID pandemic, when the general public, I have a sense the general public got a little bit confused and tired of scientists advising policymakers and then policymakers making decisions that appeared to flip flop.

You know, "now do this, now wear face masks, then maybe don’t wear face mask, maybe isolate, maybe don’t isolate.”

There were changes of recommendation and position. Now, to somebody who understands the scientific process, this is to be expected. We are in a completely new situation.

Nobody who’s alive today, who does research on the pandemic, has ever experienced a pandemic of this scale. So of course we’re learning as we go along.

It’s natural that it’s going to lead to failures, which then can be corrected.

And again, this is so crucial to emphasize it.

We learn from these failures, and the next decision, the next recommendation, is going to be better informed, better underpinned by facts.

And so taking a step back from this example, communicating that scientific process, which is all about failing, learning from failure, moving on, maybe failing again, taking a step back, taking two steps forward, maybe another step back, and and so on.

I think by missing that opportunity, we miss the opportunity to make science and scientific process more trustworthy, to show that it really is worthy of trust. We talk about trust in science a great deal, rightly so.

We are worried about the fact that trust in science is dropping.

Perhaps by embracing failure, we can reverse that trend.

We can be more transparent, more honest, and therefore bring more people along.

It’s an interesting point to consider whether a conference on failure should itself be a success or failure.

I think whatever we discuss here will be important, will be success.

And I will just end with a quote that I came across by complete coincidence in a bit of a trashy novel that I was reading on holidays recently.

I was very surprised. The quote comes from Winston Churchill, and apparently he said: "Success is the ability to go from one failure to another with no loss of enthusiasm.”

And I actually think that summarizes many of the endeavours that you all engage in, whatever you do.

rss_13_1792447726.title: Lessons from Katrina: how to rebuild academia from the ground up
rss_13_1792447726.text:
On 29 August 2005, Hurricane Katrina made landfall in southeast Louisiana as a Category 3 storm, with sustained winds of 205 kilometres per hour and a storm surge reaching between 4.6 and 5.8 metres in eastern New Orleans. The storm remains one of the deadliest ever to hit the United States, with millions of people displaced and more than 1,800 killed in the hurricane and ensuing floods. By 31 August, around 80% of New Orleans — the most affected city — was underwater.

Katrina had a profound impact city-wide, causing $17 billion in damages in Orleans Parish — the local county — alone. The burden of damage and the recovery efforts that followed fell unevenly. Environmental-justice scholars, such as Robert Bullard at Texas Southern University in Houston, argue that disasters are not great levellers, but follow lines of inequity that are already written into a city.

The academic sector suffered with the city. All ten of the main colleges and universities in the metropolitan area were affected. Some 84,000 students and 15,000 faculty members were displaced. Louisiana’s public universities collectively sustained between US$500 million and $600 million in physical damage, lost more than $150 million in tuition fees and revenue and faced $75 million in immediate budget cuts.

More than two decades on, the picture across the academic sector mirrors that of New Orleans as a whole: an uneven but impressive recovery. The reasons for divergence provide lessons for other institutions around the world looking to rebuild after a disaster.

IN SHORT Lessons in defiance after a hurricane ● Recovery takes patience: plans must span several years. ● Lean on the wider academic community: networks are invaluable to support students and staff. ● Prioritize people: academia is a small part of a larger society that is working to recover. ● Pay it forward: after recovery, consider offering educational programmes to students from other institutions that have experienced disaster. ● Academia can struggle to be heard: advocate for safeguards loudly and before disaster. ● Learn what you can: during recovery, build resilient infrastructure and create contingency plans.

A city emptied of its people

The physical damage to the city’s institutes was shaped in part by geography. Most of New Orleans sits below sea level in a natural bowl, with the higher land running alongside the riverbank.

Institutions on higher ground, such as the Uptown campuses of Tulane University and Loyola University New Orleans, remained structurally intact. But lower-lying establishments faced substantial flooding, including the Louisiana State University Health Sciences Center (LSUHSC). Also heavily affected were Dillard University, Southern University at New Orleans (SUNO) and Xavier University of Louisiana (XULA), the city’s three historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) — a category of around 100 US institutions founded before 1964, predominantly in the southern states, to educate Black students at a time when other universities excluded them.

The storm’s eye passed east of the city; the flooding was caused by the failure of federal levees and floodwalls in the Lower Ninth Ward, New Orleans East, Gentilly and Lakeview. “The first disaster was the disparate way that communities were protected by levees,” says Bullard. “Those preconditions set up the disparate impact on every aspect of Black life in New Orleans, including the HBCUs.”

Water-damaged books in a library at Dillard University in New Orleans, which was one of the historically Black colleges and universities that were disproportionately affected by Hurricane Katrina.Credit: Adam Nadel/Polaris/eyevine

The ground floor of every building on XULA’s campus was flooded with around 2 metres of water. SUNO experienced 1.2 to 3.4 metres of flooding and Dillard was submerged under more than 2 metres of water. The basements of all buildings at the LSUHSC were severely damaged and two of the city’s teaching hospitals were forced to close. (One temporarily reopened before closing permanently in 2015.)

“Low-lying [land] is one variable and one factor”, but there were others at play, Bullard says. He points to redlined neighbourhoods — those systematically disadvantaged by a federal practice of marking neighbourhoods as too risky for mortgage lending on the basis of racial or ethnic makeup, initiated in the 1930s. These areas were among the hardest hit and most likely to be denied loans. Those factors affected education, schools and universities during the recovery.

The early stages

Even before the water receded, efforts to mitigate damage had begun. At Tulane, staff spent more than two months working to save the fifth-floor nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometers. Generator-powered freight elevators allowed them to manually transport liquid nitrogen, which prevented the superconducting magnets from losing their magnetism. “There was heroism in terms of some of the researchers who were saving cell cultures, topping off nitrogen tanks and making sure all of the research stayed intact,” recalls Lee Hamm, dean of Tulane University School of Medicine, who was at the institution throughout the recovery.

All of New Orleans’s principal institutions cancelled their 2005 autumn semesters. Across the country, colleges and universities offered to take in displaced students: Princeton University in New Jersey partnered with Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, to welcome Dillard students; Loyola students were rehoused by the Association of Jesuit Colleges and Universities across their 27 member institutions; and medical students from Tulane were relocated to Baylor College of Medicine in Houston. “The money that they were paying for their tuition actually came to Tulane still, which was an unbelievable gift,” says Hamm.

Failure of federal levees and floodwalls has been blamed for the catastrophic flooding that hit New Orleans in 2005.Credit: Mark Wilson/Getty

Marguerite Giguette, provost at XULA, describes the depth of collaboration across institutions and the local community. XULA’s registrar, who evacuated to Dallas, Texas, ran operations from a university there. A hotel in central New Orleans housed students and faculty members from Dillard, one of the most affected institutions, and once XULA reopened in January 2006, it provided laboratory space for Dillard students to complete their science courses because their campus remained unusable.

XULA, Tulane, Loyola and Dillard formalized and expanded a pre-existing agreement that allowed students to take courses at neighbouring institutions at their home tuition rate. “It was a way that we could help each other with the staffing we had … and the facilities,” says Giguette. The consortium still operates today.

The rebuild

As private universities, Tulane and Loyola had insurance and large endowments to cushion the immediate blow, but many others did not, notes a 2025 analysis from the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC. For example, the city’s three HBCUs had much smaller safety nets.

Federal aid compounded existing inequities. When Congress allocated $200 million of federal disaster-relief funding to higher education in 2005, the money was split equally between Louisiana and Mississippi, even though Louisiana faced more than four times the damage of its neighbour. Smaller institutions in Louisiana, including all three of the HBCUs in New Orleans, were also disadvantaged by the formula used to allocate aid by the state’s Board of Regents — the governing body in charge of supervising higher education — thereby further under-resourcing them, notes the Brookings analysis.

“The structural inequity and the systemic inequality was pre-storm,” says Bullard. “But when [post-storm] policies got implemented, those preconditions got baked into the recovery and the resourcing of institutions.”

Then came a second blow to public institutions. In 2008, only three years into the rebuild, the global financial recession hit. Although most of Louisiana’s state spending consists of mandatory obligations, higher education is not protected by the state constitutions in the way that primary and secondary education are. Thus began a period of sustained disinvestment in public higher education in the state, which was not reversed as the economy recovered. At the University of New Orleans, for example, state funding dropped from $55.3 million in 2005 (around $90 million in 2025 when adjusted for inflation) to $30.5 million in 2025 — a 44.7% decline in nominal terms over 20 years.
